questions.stem: Under the going concern assumption, it is assumed that:
options: reports are prepared for a set period such as a year
revenue is recognised when earned, not when received
the business will continue to operate into the future
the business's records are kept separate from the owner's
questions.explanation: The going concern assumption is that the entity will not be wound up in the near future but will continue its activities. Separate records describe the entity assumption, and set periods describe the period assumption.

questions.stem: Ironbark Plumbing completes a job in June but is not paid until July. The fee is recorded as revenue in June. Which assumption or qualitative characteristic is being applied?
questions.explanation: Under the accrual basis, revenue is recognised in the period in which it is earned, regardless of when the cash arrives. The entity assumption is about keeping the owner's affairs separate, which this transaction does not involve.

questions.stem: The owner of Fern Gully Gardening pays her private health insurance from the business bank account, and the bookkeeper records it as Drawings. Which accounting assumption is applied?
questions.explanation: The entity assumption keeps the owner's personal transactions out of the business's revenue and expenses, so the payment is Drawings, not an expense. Recording it as an expense would understate the business's profit.

questions.stem: Keeping source documents so that independent observers can check that each transaction was faithfully recorded supports which qualitative characteristic?
questions.explanation: The study design states that verifiability is maintained by keeping the source documents and is checked through auditing. Timeliness is about having information in time to influence decisions.

questions.stem: A business prepares its Income Statement in the same format every year so the owner can see how each expense has changed. Which qualitative characteristic does this support?
questions.explanation: Comparability lets users identify similarities and differences between periods or between entities, which a consistent format makes possible. Verifiability depends on source documents, not on the layout of a report.

questions.stem: The owner of a yoga studio needs a report next week to decide whether to renew her lease, but her accountant can supply it only next month. Which qualitative characteristic is lacking?
questions.explanation: Information that arrives after the decision is made cannot influence it, so the report lacks timeliness. It may be clear, checkable and comparable, but it is no use to the owner if it is late.

questions.stem: To get a loan, an owner shows the bank a Balance Sheet that leaves out a large amount owed to a supplier. Which statement best describes the report?
options: It is not understandable to the bank's lending officer
It is incomplete, so it is not a faithful representation
It lacks timeliness, as it is prepared after the period
It is not comparable, as other businesses list suppliers
questions.explanation: A faithful representation must be complete, free from material error and neutral, and leaving out a liability fails all three. Nothing suggests the report was late or hard to read; the problem is what is missing.

questions.stem: Which source document is used to record a credit sale of services to a customer?
options: A copy of the sales invoice
questions.explanation: A sales invoice is issued when services are provided on credit, and the business keeps a copy as its source document. A cash receipt records money received, and a statement of account summarises a customer's balance.

questions.stem: Each month a business receives a document from a supplier listing the invoices, payments and balance owing on its account. This document is a:
questions.explanation: A statement of account summarises the transactions on an account and the balance owing for a period. A purchase invoice relates to a single purchase, and a memo is an internal document.

questions.stem: The owner of a design studio takes the business's old printer home for personal use. Which source document would record this?
questions.explanation: A memo is an internal document used to record transactions that do not involve an outside party, such as drawings of a business asset. No sale, purchase or payment took place, so the other documents do not apply.

questions.stem: A tax invoice contains the information needed for the GST system. Which item would you expect to see on a tax invoice?
options: The customer's bank account number and BSB
The supplier's current bank account balance
The supplier's personal tax file number (TFN)
questions.explanation: A tax invoice shows the supplier's ABN along with details such as the date, a description of the supply and the GST. A tax file number is private and never appears on an invoice.

questions.stem: A customer pays for a haircut with a credit card at the counter. For the hairdresser, this is:
options: a credit transaction, because the customer paid with a credit card
a credit transaction, to be recorded in the business's Sales Journal
a cash transaction, to be recorded in the business's Sales Journal
a cash transaction, as payment is received at the time of the service
questions.explanation: The business receives its money at the time of the service, so it is a cash transaction recorded in the Cash Receipts Journal. The customer owes the card provider, not the hairdresser, so no account receivable is created.

questions.stem: A business receives a $20,000 loan from its bank. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets increase by $20,000 and liabilities increase by $20,000
Assets increase by $20,000 and owner's equity increases by $20,000
Liabilities increase by $20,000 and owner's equity decreases by $20,000
Assets increase by $20,000 and liabilities decrease by $20,000
questions.explanation: Bank rises by $20,000 and the loan is a new liability of $20,000, so the equation stays in balance. Borrowed money is owed to the bank and does not increase owner's equity.

questions.stem: A business pays $3,000 in wages by EFT. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets decrease by $3,000 and owner's equity decreases by $3,000
Assets decrease by $3,000 and liabilities decrease by $3,000
Liabilities increase by $3,000 and owner's equity decreases by $3,000
One asset decreases by $3,000 and another asset increases by $3,000
questions.explanation: Bank falls by $3,000, and wages are an expense, which reduces owner's equity by $3,000. No liability was owed for these wages, so liabilities do not change.

questions.stem: Greenleaf Landscaping invoices a customer $1,100 including GST for work just completed. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets +$1,100, liabilities no change, owner's equity +$1,100
questions.explanation: Accounts Receivable rises by the full $1,100 the customer owes. The $100 of GST is owed to the ATO, so GST Clearing (a liability) rises by $100, and the $1,000 fee is revenue that increases owner's equity. GST is never revenue to the business.

questions.stem: A business receives $880 from a customer who owes it money. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets fall by $880 and owner's equity falls by $880 as an expense
Bank rises and Accounts Receivable falls, so total assets are unchanged
Assets rise by $880 and owner's equity rises by $880 as revenue
Assets rise by $880 and liabilities rise by $880 as the debt is paid
questions.explanation: Collecting a debt swaps one asset (Accounts Receivable) for another (Bank), so totals do not change. The revenue was recognised when the service was provided, so recording it again would double count it.

questions.stem: The owner of a cleaning business withdraws $500 cash from the business for personal use. What is the effect?
options: Assets −$500 and owner's equity −$500, with no effect on profit
Assets −$500 and owner's equity −$500, as a $500 expense
Assets −$500 and liabilities −$500, with no effect on profit
Liabilities +$500 and owner's equity −$500, as a $500 expense
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce Bank and reduce owner's equity directly. They are a distribution to the owner, not an expense, so they do not reduce profit. Treating drawings as an expense is a common error that understates profit.

questions.stem: Which transaction increases cash but does not affect profit?
options: Receiving a loan from the bank
questions.explanation: A loan brings in cash but is a liability, not revenue, so profit is unchanged. Providing services earns revenue, which does affect profit whether paid now or later.

questions.stem: Which transaction reduces profit but has no immediate effect on cash?
options: Receiving an invoice for advertising, to be paid next month
Paying wages to staff by EFT at the end of the week
Repaying part of a bank loan by direct debit
The owner withdrawing cash for personal use
questions.explanation: The advertising expense is incurred now, so it reduces profit now, but the cash is paid later. Paying wages reduces both, while loan repayments and drawings reduce cash without being expenses.

questions.stem: In March, a cleaning business earned fees of $12,000 (excluding GST), of which $9,000 was on credit. It collected $5,000 from customers for February work, paid expenses of $7,000 in cash, and the owner withdrew $2,000. What is the net profit for March?
questions.explanation: Under the accrual basis, profit = fees earned in March $12,000 − expenses incurred $7,000 = $5,000. The February collection was earned last month, and drawings are not an expense. Using cash received ($3,000 + $5,000) less cash paid gives $1,000, which is not profit.

questions.stem: Pinnacle Physio made a net loss for the year, yet its bank balance increased. Which transaction could explain this?
options: It paid off a large amount owed to its suppliers
It bought new treatment equipment for cash
Its owner withdrew cash for personal use
It borrowed $50,000 from its bank during the year
questions.explanation: A loan brings cash in without being revenue, so cash can rise while the business makes a loss. Paying suppliers, buying equipment and drawings all reduce cash, so none could explain a rise.

questions.stem: How does a service business differ from a trading business?
options: It does not need to buy any materials or supplies
It does not charge GST on the fees that it earns
It earns its revenue from providing services, not selling inventory
It never makes credit sales to any of its customers
questions.explanation: A service business earns fees for work done, while a trading business buys and resells goods. Service businesses still make credit sales, buy materials and supplies, and charge GST on most fees.

questions.stem: A mobile dog groomer buys shampoo and conditioner that are used up washing customers' dogs. For this business, these items are:
options: drawings, as they are not sold to customers directly
materials and supplies used in providing the service
inventory held for resale to the business's customers
non-current assets that will be used for several years
questions.explanation: Shampoo used up in grooming is consumed in providing the service, so it is materials and supplies, not inventory for resale. It is used within months, not years, so it is not a non-current asset.

questions.stem: A tutoring business's fees revenue rose by 10%, but the number of returning students fell by a third. What should the owner conclude?
options: The business is performing well, as revenue has increased
Non-financial indicators are irrelevant when revenue rises
The fall in students shows that net profit has already fallen
Future revenue may be at risk, as customer loyalty is falling
questions.explanation: Fewer returning students is a non-financial warning sign that revenue may fall in later periods, even though it rose this year. Profit depends on expenses as well, so the student numbers alone cannot show that net profit has already fallen.

questions.stem: A web design business has fees of $150,000 and average total assets of $60,000. What is its asset turnover?
questions.explanation: Asset turnover = net sales ÷ average total assets = 150,000 ÷ 60,000 = 2.5 times, so each dollar of assets generated $2.50 of fees. Dividing assets by fees gives 0.4, which inverts the indicator.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of special journals?
options: To record the closing entries for revenue and expenses at the period end
To summarise the assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a given date
To replace the need for the business to keep any source documents
To group frequent, similar transactions so they can be recorded efficiently
questions.explanation: Special journals collect transactions of the same type, such as cash receipts, in columns so totals can be posted together. Source documents are still needed as evidence for every entry.

questions.stem: A business pays its electricity bill by EFT. In which journal is this recorded?
questions.explanation: Every payment of money is recorded in the Cash Payments Journal. The Purchases Journal records only purchases on credit, where payment happens later.

questions.stem: A business buys office stationery on credit and receives a purchase invoice. In which journal is this recorded?
questions.explanation: Credit purchases are recorded in the Purchases Journal from the purchase invoice. The Cash Payments Journal is used later, when the supplier is paid.

questions.stem: A customer pays an amount owing by EFT. Where is this recorded?
options: The Cash Receipts Journal, in the Accounts Receivable column
The Sales Journal, in the Accounts Receivable column
The Cash Receipts Journal, in the Fees column
The Cash Payments Journal, in the Accounts Receivable column
questions.explanation: Money received goes in the Cash Receipts Journal, and because it settles an existing debt it goes in the Accounts Receivable column. Putting it in the Fees column would record the revenue a second time.

questions.stem: A credit service of $660 including GST is recorded in the Sales Journal. Which amounts are entered?
questions.explanation: The customer owes the GST-inclusive $660. GST is one-eleventh of the inclusive price, $60, leaving fees of $600. Taking 10% of $660 gives $66, which overstates the GST.

questions.stem: Which is an internal control procedure to safeguard cash?
options: Having one person receive, record and bank all cash
Keeping the day's takings in an unlocked drawer
Destroying source documents after recording them
questions.explanation: Banking daily limits the cash on the premises that could be stolen. Having one person handle every step removes the cross-checks that would reveal theft or fraud.

questions.stem: A business makes sure that the employee who receives cash is not the employee who records it. This separation of duties mainly reduces the risk of:
options: the business running short of cash
questions.explanation: When two people are involved, one would have to work with the other to steal and hide it, so fraud is harder and more likely to be found. Separation of duties does not affect how quickly customers pay.

questions.stem: At a small accounting practice, the bookkeeper both approves supplier invoices and makes the EFT payments, with no one checking her work. Which risk is greatest?
options: Fees revenue being recorded in the wrong period
Equipment purchases being recorded as expenses
Payments to a fictitious supplier going unnoticed
Customers being overcharged GST on their invoices
questions.explanation: Someone who can both approve and pay invoices can create a fake supplier and pay it without anyone noticing. Separating approval from payment, or reviewing payments, is the control that addresses this.

questions.stem: In the Cash Flow Statement, cash drawings by the owner are reported under:
questions.explanation: Drawings change the owner's investment in the business, so they are a financing activity, like capital contributions. They are not an expense and are never part of operating activities.

questions.stem: A business buys a new computer for cash. Where is this payment reported in the Cash Flow Statement?
questions.explanation: Payments for non-current assets are investing activities. Operating activities cover day-to-day trading, such as receipts from customers and payments for wages.

questions.stem: Interest paid on a bank loan is reported in which section of the Cash Flow Statement?
options: None, as it is an expense
questions.explanation: Interest is a cost of running the business, so it is reported with operating activities; only the repayment of the loan itself is financing. The interest is also an expense in the Income Statement, but it is still a cash outflow.

questions.stem: A service business's cash flows for the year were: receipts from customers $50,000; GST received $5,000; payments to suppliers $18,000; GST paid $1,800; wages $20,000; purchase of equipment $9,000; drawings $12,000. What is the net cash flow from operating activities?
questions.explanation: Operating activities are 50,000 + 5,000 − 18,000 − 1,800 − 20,000 = $15,200. Leaving out the GST lines gives $12,000. The equipment is investing and drawings are financing, so neither belongs in operating activities.

questions.stem: A business's records for the year show fees $95,000, wages $40,000, rent $18,000, advertising $4,000, drawings $25,000 and a loan repayment of $6,000. What is the net profit?
questions.explanation: Net profit = fees $95,000 − expenses ($40,000 + $18,000 + $4,000) = $33,000. Drawings and loan repayments reduce cash but are not expenses, so subtracting them gives the wrong figures.

questions.stem: Opening capital was $60,000. During the year the business earned a net profit of $33,000, the owner withdrew $25,000 and contributed a further $10,000. What is closing capital in the Balance Sheet?
questions.explanation: Closing capital = 60,000 + 10,000 + 33,000 − 25,000 = $78,000. Forgetting the contribution gives $68,000, and leaving out drawings gives $103,000.

questions.stem: At the end of the year, GST Clearing has a credit balance. In the classified Balance Sheet it is reported as:
questions.explanation: A credit balance means the business has collected more GST than it has paid, so it owes the difference to the ATO within months. GST collected belongs to the ATO, so it is never revenue.

questions.stem: Which type of graph best shows the trend in a business's monthly fees over two years?
questions.explanation: A line graph plots values over time, so rises and falls from month to month are easy to see. A pie chart shows parts of a whole at one point in time and cannot show a trend.

questions.stem: Which type of graph best shows each expense's share of a business's total expenses for one year?
questions.explanation: A pie chart divides a whole into parts, so each expense appears as its share of the total. A line graph shows change over time, and a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables.

questions.stem: The owner of a small business records the cost of a family holiday as a business travel expense. What is the effect on the reports?
options: Expenses overstated, net profit understated and less tax paid
Expenses understated, net profit overstated and more tax paid
Assets overstated, owner's equity overstated, profit unchanged
Revenue overstated, net profit overstated, drawings understated
questions.explanation: A private holiday is Drawings, so recording it as an expense overstates expenses and understates profit, which reduces the tax payable. As well as breaching the entity assumption, it is unethical and illegal.

questions.stem: A customer offers an electrician a lower price if he does a job for cash without issuing an invoice, so the job is never recorded. If he agrees, the business's reports will show:
options: understated fees revenue and net profit
overstated fees revenue and cash at bank
overstated GST collected for the ATO
questions.explanation: An unrecorded job leaves out revenue, so fees and profit are understated, and GST owed to the ATO is not reported. This avoids tax and breaches faithful representation, as well as being unethical.
